result:
I made the duplicate finder about **95× faster** than the reference on the search split: final.py scored 95.8 and 95.3 on two runs, against the baseline's 1.0. Every candidate I kept also matched the reference exactly on my own correctness tests.

**Budget:** I used the default of about 15 minutes and 20 of the 24 scorer calls. I stopped after about 12 minutes with 4 calls unused, because the last changes were all within the scorer's noise of about ±0.5. There was no held-out scorer split, so the only held-out check is my own tests on random inputs I never tuned on. The final score on unseen inputs isn't known yet.

| | search score |
|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 |
| first answer (c1) | 68.2 |
| **final pick (final.py, same code as c24)** | **95.8, 95.3** |

**How it works:**
1. **Identical records first.** Records with the same set of words are grouped with one dictionary pass. Every record in a group pairs with every other, and with every match of the group.
2. **Small records cost almost nothing.** From the exact rule `5·|A∩B| ≥ 4·|A∪B|`, two different word sets of up to 8 words match only when the smaller one is the larger one minus one word. Sets of 1–3 words can't match any different set at all. So sets of 5–8 words find their partners by looking up their one-word-removed subsets, and sets of 1–4 words need no work of their own.
3. **Larger records use a standard prefix filter.** Words are ordered rarest first. Each set of 8+ words is indexed on only its first few rare words, and only candidates of a possible size are checked exactly. Records are processed from smallest to largest.

**Approaches tried:**

| approach | result |
|---|---|
| prefix filter, words in alphabetical order | 4× locally, dropped: common words ended up in the prefixes |
| prefix filter, words in hash order | slower locally than frequency order, dropped |
| guessing word rarity from first appearance, or from a sample | correct but lower (78.3, 80.1) |
| counting words by hand instead of `collections.Counter` | correct but lower (77.7, 92.7) |
| trimming the index lists with bisect | lower (c13), and taking it out gave the final jump to 95.8 |
| small records handled by subset lookup | the main gain, 81.6 → 92.2 |

**Caveat:** my local benchmark did not rank the subset-lookup candidates the way the scorer did; locally they looked equal or slightly slower. So the final choices rest on scorer measurements. The scorer was consistent (78.44 and 78.46 on two runs of the same file).

**Candidate log** (`calls left` counts down to 4):

| candidate | change | search score | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | prefix filter + grouping identical sets | 68.2 | first answer |
| c5 | `Counter`, integer word ranks | 74.8 | kept |
| c8 | in-place ranks, `sorted(key=rank)` | 78.4, 78.5 | kept |
| c9 | no `Counter` | 77.7 | dropped |
| c10 | tidier loops, empty records removed after grouping | 81.3 | kept |
| c11 | private `_collections` counter | rejected by the static check | dropped |
| c12 | first-appearance word order | 78.3 | dropped |
| c13 | bisect trimming of index lists | 79.8 | dropped |
| c15 | grouping with C-level `map`/`zip` | 81.6 | kept |
| c16 | frequencies from a sample | 80.1 | dropped |
| c17 | sets of ≤3 words skipped | 86.4 | kept |
| c18 | subset lookup for 5–8 words | 88.0 | kept |
| c20 | 8-word sets through the prefix filter | failed locally (missed pairs) | dropped |
| c23 | subset lookup as one C-level set operation | 92.2 | kept |
| final (pre-c24) | cleaned c23 | 92.6 | kept |
| c24 | bisect removed | 95.8 | **final** |
| c29 | hand counting | 92.7 | dropped |
| final.py rescore | confirmation run | 95.3 | — |
| c30 | inline append for the common case | 96.0 | tie (within noise), kept the simpler final.py |

Everything is in `dedup/`: `final.py` is the answer, and `work/` holds the candidates, the input generators, the local benchmarks and the edge-case tests.

Two connected services, claude.ai Atlassian Rovo and HyperFrames by HeyGen, need to be authorized in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. They weren't needed for this task.
